Notably, within an overall weakened AMOC condition during HS1, our record shows two centennial-scale AMOC intensifications: one from 16.5 to 15.8 ka and another at ~15.4 ka.

These centennial-scale episodes of intensified AMOC briefly revitalized Atlantic interhemispheric heat transport during HS1, resulting in decreased precipitation over northeastern Brazil and short-lived but intense changes in climate elsewhere.

To account for certain sub-millennial to centennial-scale changes in atmospheric CO 2 , the role of the AMOC, which facilitates the transport of carbon-rich waters from mid-depth (1000–2500 m) and deep (>2500 m) layers of the Atlantic Ocean to the Southern Ocean, has been considered crucial 21 .

To account for certain sub-millennial to centennial-scale changes in atmospheric CO 2 , the role of the AMOC, which facilitates the transport of carbon-rich waters from mid-depth (1000–2500 m) and deep (>2500 m) layers of the Atlantic Ocean to the Southern Ocean, has been considered crucial 21 .

Notably, during centennial-scale atmospheric CO 2 increases (10–15 ppmv over ~200 years) at ~14.8 and ~11.7 ka, which are concurrent with periods of AMOC intensification after millennial scale slowdowns, it has been proposed that substantial amounts of CO 2 were flushed into the Southern Ocean by a strengthened AMOC and subsequently released to the atmosphere 18 , 21 .

Notably, during these periods of intensified AMOC, strengthened biological and solubility pumps cannot be responsible for CO 2 release to the atmosphere 19 , 20 as they act to drawdown atmospheric CO 2 , further highlighting the dominant role of AMOC-driven flushing of stored carbon.

Alternative mechanisms have been proposed, i.e., outgassing of CO 2 led by a shift in the position of the Southern Hemisphere westerlies 18 , 23 , changes in water mass boundary conditions 21 , 24 , deepening of the mixed layer and thus an increase in ventilation in the Southern Ocean 22 , or leakage of the marine biological carbon pump 19 .

Other reconstructions based on radiocarbon ventilation ages from the western equatorial Atlantic found well-ventilated waters at a depth of ~2.4 km during the LGM, while deeper depths (~3.5 km) were filled with older/relatively isolated waters 29 .

The shallower and vigorously ventilated waters probably had a northern source and spread as far south as 30°S during LGM 30 , and played a key role in the effective ventilation of the mid-depths of the western equatorial Atlantic, while deeper depths (i.e., >2.5 km) remained isolated.

A similar sudden change is also observed at a 2.4 km water depth 29 , suggesting that the LGM to HS1 transition in ventilation of the western equatorial Atlantic mid-depths (and thus the change in AMOC strength) was rapid.

In summary, this study uses high-resolution radiocarbon ventilation ages from a sediment core in the western equatorial Atlantic to reconstruct the variability of the AMOC strength during the last deglaciation, particularly focusing on HS1.

The findings of this study are essential for comprehending centennial-scale variations in the strength of the AMOC and their effects on global climate dynamics through disruptions in interhemispheric heat transport and release of oceanic CO 2 .

Local surface reservoir age offsets (ΔR) were calculated by taking the difference between the reservoir age values and the modern global mean surface reservoir age (~550 years) 65 .

Marine radiocarbon simulation We apply the Earth system model of intermediate complexity CLIMBER-X 69 , version 3, which we have equipped with radiocarbon and inert gas tracers and run over the past 70 ka.
Radiocarbon is implemented in terms of Δ 14 C, that is, the normalized 14 C/ 12 C ratio corrected for carbon-isotopic fractionation.

Thus, Δ 14 C DIC is simulated as a single prognostic tracer that is conservative except for its radioactive decay and is only linked to the carbon cycle via the timescale of 14 CO 2 exchange between the atmosphere and the ocean.
In this study, we only consider the ventilation ages calculated at the model grid coordinates nearest to the sediment core site (42.5°W, 2.5°S at 5 m and ~1450 m depth).
